system.summary: Item A: numbers 1-65 single letters with 2-3 homophones, 66-455 an alphabetical table of syllables and words (82 able ... 455 you), 460-506 number codes; items B-D unseen.
system.notes: System fields describe item A (no. 52) only. The four letters are probably four different ciphers; split them once B-D are seen.

prior_solution.where: Davys, An Essay on the Art of Decyphering (London 1737) pp. 24-29, for item A only

conditions.human_role: Pasted the catalogue task; no other input.

solution.what: Digital Bodleian and EMLO: no images of MS. e Mus. 203 or Eng. misc. e. 475. Auction photographs (8) fetched: none shows letters 50-53.
Dominic Winter lot 375 description: Davys 1737 printed the Buckingham letter (no. 52). Davys 1737 found on archive.org: letter 52 printed with interlinear decipherment, key and notes (pp. 24-29).
Thurloe SP i (April 1653) searched for a Brasset to Bordeaux clear copy as a crib for no. 50: none.
Letter 52 transcribed from Davys's page images with his reading aligned group for group (letter52_davys.txt, letter52_ct.txt).

check52.py: key built from the alignment; clashes only case, i/I and u/v, plus two forced values (118 county/counte-, 144 dy/di); letters 1-65 homophonic, 66-455 alphabetical syllable/word table. 456/480 groups read (95.0%).

Open names placed by the alphabetical table: 71 (a-block, Argyle fits), 254 (between lord and London, an L name), 277 (between ly and man: Leslie per Davys, or Massey). Not decided; not written into the reading.

outcome.method_basis: Item A was deciphered in print by John Davys (1737); here it was transcribed from the printed page images and checked for consistency. Items B-D were not seen.

texts.label: no. 52, Buckingham to an English royalist (Lancashire rising), 1651; Davys 1737 pp. 24-25
texts.summary: The Lancashire gentlemen are ready to rise for the King and ask for a party of horse from Scotland to countenance their rising; the Lords in Scotland promise their best horse and Highland foot under 277 and Buckingham; Buckingham has leave to raise a troop of English horse and will go that way into England rather than lie disguised about London; the bearer Colonel Berkenhead, main negotiator of the Lancashire business, will give a full account.
